**For a typical full-size fridge, get about 1,000 Wh for most of a day or about 1,500 Wh for a full 24 hours, plus at least about 1,500 W of continuous output.** A station has to pass three checks.

## The three checks

1. **Surge (startup) watts.** This is the check that most often fails. When the compressor kicks on, it briefly draws several times its running power. Sources disagree on how much: about 900–1,200 W ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)), a 1,300 W allowance ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)), or up to 1,200–2,400 W for large or older fridges ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). A station with roughly 1,500 W or more of continuous output covers almost any home fridge.
2. **Continuous watts and pure sine wave.** A fridge only draws about 100–250 W while running, so almost any 1,000 W-class station handles it. The station should output pure sine wave power, which reputable brands do ([BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [Anker](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).
3. **Capacity (Wh), which sets how long it runs.** The compressor only runs about a third of the time, so the average draw is much lower than the running watts. A typical ENERGY STAR full-size fridge uses 362 kWh per year, which averages about 41 W or about 1,000 Wh per day. After inverter losses and a 20% safety margin, that becomes about **1,400 Wh per day** ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

**To estimate for your own fridge:** find the kWh/year figure on the yellow EnergyGuide label.
- Average watts = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760
- Wh you need = average watts × 24 × days ÷ 0.85 × 1.2

Big side-by-sides with ice makers can use twice the typical amount. Keeping the door shut stretches runtime a lot.

## Picks by outage length

**About 1 kWh (most of a day, 12–17 hours)**
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2**: 1,070 Wh, about $499. HomeGrid estimates about 17 hours on a typical fridge. [Check price](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
- **BLUETTI AC180**: 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous and 2,700 W peak. Seen at $399–699. [Check price](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)

**About 1.5 kWh (a full 24 hours)**
- **Anker SOLIX F1500**: 1,536 Wh, 1,800 W continuous and 2,400 W surge. It was $599.99 at Anker as of Oct 22. [See it](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)

**About 2 kWh (a day and a half, or a fridge plus other essentials)**
- **BLUETTI AC200L**: 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous. It expands to 8 kWh with add-on batteries, so you can extend it for longer outages later.
  - Price: $899 at BLUETTI's store. Code **AFF5OFF** took off $44.95, bringing it to $854.05, in a cart test on 2026-10-21. [Buy at BLUETTI](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l)
  - That link is an affiliate link ([details](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l)).
  - Its 3,600 W "Power Lifting" figure is meant for heaters and similar loads, not motor startup. The 2,400 W continuous rating already clears any fridge.
- **Anker SOLIX S2000**: 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W continuous and 3,000 W peak. $699.99 after coupon. [Shop at Anker](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)

## Tips
- **Test it before an outage.** Plug the fridge in and let the compressor cycle a few times to confirm the station doesn't trip.
- **Check food temperature.** USDA guidance: food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **Plan for longer outages.** For multi-day outages, choose an expandable unit or add solar charging.

If you share your fridge's kWh/year figure and how long your outages usually last, I can narrow this down to one pick.
